questions.stem:
The table shows the production (in tonnes) of cereals from 2019 to 2024 in a village.

| Year | Rice | Wheat | Barley | Oats | Maize |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2019 | 2415 | 825 | 530 | 410 | 740 |
| 2020 | 2320 | 940 | 480 | 590 | 760 |
| 2021 | 2617 | 1060 | 460 | 610 | 775 |
| 2022 | 2720 | 1120 | 520 | 630 | 790 |
| 2023 | 2516 | 1040 | 670 | 720 | 810 |
| 2024 | 2810 | 960 | 720 | 810 | 825 |

In the year 2022, the cereal that yielded the highest growth percent over the previous year is
questions.explanation:
Compare each cereal's 2022 figure with its 2021 figure:

| Cereal | 2021 → 2022 | Growth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rice | 2617 → 2720 | 3.9% |
| Wheat | 1060 → 1120 | 5.7% |
| **Barley** | 460 → 520 | **13.0%** |
| Oats | 610 → 630 | 3.3% |
| Maize | 775 → 790 | 1.9% |

**Barley** wins easily: its absolute rise of 60 tonnes is small, but so is its base — the point of a *percentage* growth question.

| 2021 | 2617 | 1060 | 460 | 610 | 775 |
| 2022 | 2720 | 1120 | 520 | 630 | 790 |
| 2023 | 2516 | 1040 | 670 | 720 | 810 |
| 2024 | 2810 | 960 | 720 | 810 | 825 |

The percentage of increase in rice production in 2024 over 2023 is approximately
questions.explanation:
Rice rose from 2516 to 2810:
$$\frac{2810 - 2516}{2516} \times 100 = \frac{294}{2516} \times 100 \approx 11.7\%,$$
which matches the option **11.66**.

*(The base must be the earlier year, 2023; dividing by 2810 instead gives 10.5%.)*

questions.stem:
A pie chart shows the marks obtained by a student in five subjects, out of a total of 900 marks, as sector angles:

| Subject | Sector angle |
| --- | --- |
| Telugu | $40^\circ$ |
| English | $80^\circ$ |
| Mathematics | $90^\circ$ |
| Physics | $70^\circ$ |
| Chemistry | the remaining sector |

The total marks obtained in the two languages is
questions.explanation:
The two languages are Telugu $(40^\circ)$ and English $(80^\circ)$, together $120^\circ$ of the $360^\circ$ circle:
$$\frac{120}{360} \times 900 = \mathbf{300} \text{ marks}.$$

*(Equivalently each degree is worth $\frac{900}{360} = 2.5$ marks, so $120 \times 2.5 = 300$.)*

questions.stem:
A pie chart shows the marks obtained by a student in five subjects, out of a total of 900 marks, as sector angles:

| Subject | Sector angle |
| --- | --- |
| Telugu | $40^\circ$ |
| English | $80^\circ$ |
| Mathematics | $90^\circ$ |
| Physics | $70^\circ$ |
| Chemistry | the remaining sector |

Marks obtained in Chemistry are
questions.explanation:
Chemistry takes whatever is left of the circle:
$$360^\circ - (40 + 80 + 90 + 70) = 360 - 280 = 80^\circ.$$

Each degree is worth $\dfrac{900}{360} = 2.5$ marks, so
$$80 \times 2.5 = \mathbf{200} \text{ marks}.$$

| Subject | Sector angle |

| Telugu | $40^\circ$ |
| English | $80^\circ$ |
| Mathematics | $90^\circ$ |
| Physics | $70^\circ$ |
| Chemistry | the remaining sector |

The marks in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry put together is
questions.explanation:
Those three sectors are $90^\circ$, $70^\circ$ and (by subtraction) $80^\circ$, totalling $240^\circ$:
$$\frac{240}{360} \times 900 = \mathbf{600} \text{ marks}.$$

*(Equivalently they occupy two-thirds of the circle, and two-thirds of 900 is 600.)*

questions.stem:
A Venn diagram gives the percentage of people speaking different languages in a city — English, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam and Tamil — with Spanish speakers shown outside all five circles. The regions carry these percentages:

| Region | % |
| --- | --- |
| English only | 10 |
| Hindi only | 9 |
| Telugu only | 4 |
| Malayalam only | 8 |
| Tamil only | 4 |
| Spanish (outside all five) | 3 |
| English and Hindi | 4 |
| English and Malayalam | 8 |
| Hindi and Telugu | 10 |
| Hindi and Malayalam | 5 |
| Hindi and Tamil | 9 |
| Telugu and Tamil | 3 |
| Malayalam and Tamil | 2 |
| English, Hindi and Malayalam | 6 |
| Hindi, Telugu and Tamil | 8 |
| Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam and Tamil | 7 |

The total population of the city is **2,00,000**.

Find the number of people who speak at least three languages.
questions.explanation:
"At least three" means every region covering three **or more** circles:
$$\underbrace{6}_{\text{Eng+Hin+Mal}} + \underbrace{8}_{\text{Hin+Tel+Tam}} + \underbrace{7}_{\text{four languages}} = 21\%.$$

$$0.21 \times 200000 = \mathbf{42000}.$$

*(The four-language region must be counted — "at least three" includes it.)*

Find the number of people who can speak exactly any two languages.
questions.explanation:
Add only the regions lying in **exactly two** circles:
$$4 + 8 + 10 + 5 + 9 + 3 + 2 = 41\%.$$

$$0.41 \times 200000 = \mathbf{82000}.$$

*(The triple and quadruple regions are excluded — "exactly two" is stricter than "at least two".)*

Find the number of people who can speak only one language.
questions.explanation:
Add the five single-language regions **and** the Spanish speakers, who also speak just one language:
$$10 + 9 + 4 + 8 + 4 + 3 = 38\%.$$

$$0.38 \times 200000 = \mathbf{76000}.$$

*(Forgetting the 3% outside the circles gives 35% and the wrong answer — they sit outside the five circles precisely because they speak only Spanish.)*

Find the number of people in the city who cannot speak Hindi.
questions.explanation:
Add every region that **includes** Hindi:
$$9 + 4 + 10 + 5 + 9 + 6 + 8 + 7 = 58\%.$$

So those who cannot speak Hindi make up
$$100 - 58 = 42\%, \qquad 0.42 \times 200000 = \mathbf{84000}.$$

*(Working with the complement is quicker than adding the non-Hindi regions one by one, and less error-prone.)*
